name: Iris Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Iris, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can give me your public line and your private view. To start, what's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy at Voltmark Components. We distribute chips, connectors and capacitors to about 400 electronics makers. Mornings I check the shortage alerts and price feeds, because component prices jump overnight. Then I haggle with brokers, approve rush orders, and decide how much to stockpile. I use AI every day to read data sheets and summarise market news, so I get through it faster than I did three years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being first to see a shortage coming and getting stock before a competitor does. It feels like a chess game. What wears me out is the pace. A fire in a factory in Asia and my whole week is rewritten. I'm 43, my partner Tomas is a hospital nurse, we have Jonah and Ada and a mortgage, and we're not rich, so a bad stretch hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I've been seeing for a while. It's a handy tool, but it doesn't change the game. At work I'd tell the team to keep using it for data sheets and keep humans on the big decisions. Online, I'd probably say nothing, it's not a debate I'd join.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is safe in that world, and I'm good at using the tools so I'd be a step ahead. What nags me is money and my employer. Voltmark's customers are in cycles, and a downturn in electronics hits us fast. We have about four months saved, which feels thin when you've got two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd get better at using the tools. I'd ask to lead a project on predictive shortage alerts, which is the bit of my job that's most valuable. I'd save an extra 250 a month, and think about renting out our spare room for extra income, since Tomas works nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Steady. I'd still wake up some nights and think about the customer cycles, but I'd go back to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. How would a plateau change your daily work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably read the same number of data sheets in half the time, and use the saved time to talk with the brokers, which gets me better prices. The AI is like a good intern. You still check it, but it saves hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the one thing still bothering you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Voltmark's order book. If a big customer moved production out of the country, it'd hit our volume, and they'd cut purchasing first. That has nothing to do with AI. That's how cyclical this business is, and it's why I keep a spare plan in my head at all times.

say: AI is a **handy tool** but it doesn't change the game.
I'd tell the team to keep humans on the **big decisions**.
think: My job is safe, and I'm a step ahead because I use the tools **well**.
What nags me is **money** and Voltmark's customer cycles, with four months saved.
do: Ask to lead a project on **predictive shortage alerts**, the most valuable part of my job.
Save an extra **250 a month** and consider renting out our spare room.
feel: **Steady**, with a night-time thought about customer cycles.
S0.quote: If a big customer moved production out of the country, it'd hit our volume, and they'd cut purchasing first.
fieldNote: Iris is **calm** because her job and her skills line up, though she names the cyclical business as the worry.
She calls AI a good **intern**, which shows her ease with it.

steps.text: Lead a project on predictive component shortage alerts
Rent out the spare room for extra income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change and we need to get ahead of it. At work I'd say we should redesign jobs on purpose, before the software does it for us. I'd tell friends to start using the tools now, because it's much easier to learn when you're not forced to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm worried even though I'm ahead. I know how fast the tools are, because I see the demos. Parts of my job will be done by a program, and I might become the person who supervises it, which needs fewer people. I could be one of the two buyers left from five. I could also be one who's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean in hard. I'd build more automations for the team, so that I'm the one who owns them. I'd write a proposal for an in-house purchasing intelligence role, and pitch it to the director. And I'd update my resume and talk to two recruiters I know in the semiconductor world, in case Voltmark doesn't bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervy but alive. There's a strange thrill to being close to it. I'd be like someone standing at the front of a wave, enjoying the speed and aware I could fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take on first if software did the checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First the data sheets and market summaries, which I already hand off. Next the routine reorders and price comparisons. Last would be the negotiation with brokers when a shortage hits, because those are tense, human calls, and they trust me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Voltmark would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The newer buyers, Pavel and Hana, who are 26 and 29. Their jobs are the routine parts, and they haven't built supplier trust yet. I'd try to teach them the tools and bring them into the projects so they're not just replaceable. But I can't protect them if the company decides to cut.

say: It's a real change, so **redesign jobs** on purpose before the software does it for us.
I'd tell friends to use the tools **now**.
think: Even ahead, I could be one of the **two buyers** left from five, or the one gone.
Newer buyers **Pavel and Hana** are the most exposed.
do: Build **automations** I own and pitch an in-house purchasing intelligence role.
Update my resume and talk to **two recruiters** in semiconductors.
feel: **Nervy but alive**, with a thrill at being close to it.
S1.quote: I'd be like someone standing at the front of a wave, enjoying the speed and aware I could fall.
fieldNote: Iris knows the tools' speed from **demos**, so her anxiety is informed rather than vague.
She tries to **protect juniors** by bringing them into projects, while admitting she can't if the company cuts.

steps.text: Build automations for the team that I own
Pitch a purchasing intelligence role to the director
Teach Pavel and Hana to use the tools on live orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we need a global plan and we need it now. At work I'd tell leadership we have to protect people in the transition, with retraining and notice. Online I'd say governments should create a bridge fund. I wouldn't argue about whether it's good or bad. It's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is thinking work and I think it ends around 2028. I'd be competing with a system that reads every price, every shortage and every contract in seconds. Even being good with the tools doesn't save me, because there's no need for a human at all. We have four months saved and a mortgage, so I'd be in trouble by next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd try to land a role as the person who oversees the AI at Voltmark, knowing it's a short-lived one. I'd cut costs hard, rent the spare room, pause holidays. I'd talk to Tomas about taking extra nursing shifts, since healthcare is hands-on and lasts. And I'd look for a trade skill we could learn, or start a business that needs people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. A cold, clear fear, not noisy. I'd keep working because that's what I do, but I'd be calculating the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Tomas, my job probably disappears in two years. You're safer than I am. We'll tighten up, we'll rent out the room, and we'll look at your night shifts. He'd say we've got through a lot and we'll get through this. Then I'd cry a bit in the bathroom, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change if it came in two years rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I have no time to retrain properly. I know the tools better than most, and I'd still just be a person in a line for fewer roles. In a longer version I could build a career in AI oversight. In two years, there's no career, only a bridge.

say: We need a **global plan** now, with retraining and notice for people in the transition.
I'd say governments should create a **bridge fund**.
think: Buying is thinking work and I think it **ends** around 2028.
With four months saved, I'd be in **trouble** by next autumn.
do: Try to land the role overseeing the **AI** at Voltmark, knowing it is short-lived.
Cut costs, rent the **spare room** and ask Tomas about extra nursing shifts.
feel: **Frightened**, a cold and clear fear that I'd manage quietly.
S2.quote: Even being good with the tools doesn't save me, because there's no need for a human at all.
fieldNote: Iris's skill with AI gives her **no comfort** here: she sees the oversight role as a bridge, not a career.
She is calm on the surface and admits she would **cry in private**, which is honest.

steps.text: Pitch myself as the AI oversight lead at Voltmark
Rent out the spare room and pause the holiday
Ask Tomas to pick up extra nursing shifts
Look at a trade course or a people-based business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a window and we should use it. At work I'd propose we set up an internal retraining program, with Voltmark paying part. Online I'd share what I learn about AI tools and tell people that the early adopters get the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I can build something that isn't a desk job, or at least a desk job in a different shape. I'd be 48. I'd want to be an AI-supply-chain consultant, or have my own small business by then. I think I can do it, but I'd want a nest egg first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one: finish a data and supply chain analytics certificate, and automate my own work so I look indispensable. Year two: start consulting on the side, with two or three small electronics firms who can't afford a full buyer. I'd save to a 9-month cushion and pay the mortgage down. And I'd get Tomas to look at a nurse practitioner course to boost his income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mixed with uneasy. It feels a bit like being in a start-up. You know there's risk, and you know the reward is bigger if you move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm only defending. With five years I can start a business. The money side matters. I'd want about nine months of expenses before I jumped, and that takes maybe two years to build at 250 a month plus the room rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you manage the mortgage over that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the regular payments, then use the rent and savings to build the buffer. I wouldn't prepay the mortgage until I had the nine months in cash. Cash gives me options. A paid-down house doesn't pay the electricity bill.

say: It's a **window** and we should use it, with Voltmark paying part of a retraining program.
I'd tell people early adopters get the **cushion**.
think: Five years lets me build something that isn't a **desk job**, or a desk job in a different shape.
I think I can do it, but I'd want a **nest egg** first.
do: Finish a data and supply chain **analytics certificate** and start consulting on the side.
Build a **nine-month** cash cushion before paying the mortgage down.
feel: **Excited and uneasy**, like being in a start-up.
S3.quote: With two years I'm only defending. With five years I can start a business.
fieldNote: Iris turns the extra time into a **business plan**: consulting, certificate and a cash buffer.
She puts **cash before mortgage prepayment**, which shows how she thinks about risk.

steps.text: Finish a data and supply chain analytics certificate
Start consulting for two small electronics firms
Build nine months of cash before prepaying the mortgage
Automate my own reporting work at Voltmark

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's build things properly. At work I'd suggest we plan skills over the next few years and look at which roles will still need people. Online I'd talk about the opportunity as well as the risk, because there's a lot of both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd be 53 when it arrives, and with ten years I can make a career move, build savings and see where the dust lands. The thinking part of my job will go, but I'll have had time to pivot into something I choose. That's a different kind of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools heavily and keep my name as the person who understands them. I'd start a small consulting practice around 2030, and invest in index funds and maybe a small rental. I'd pay the mortgage down steadily. And I'd keep my skills fresh, because that's my insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'd treat it as a long project. It's a lot less stressful when you know the date is far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still move early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not in a panic. I'd get a good base first, then move around year four or five. Moving early means I'm choosing, not being chosen. It's a bit like selling a house before the market turns, you get the better price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonah and Ada about careers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn how to learn. And to be curious about people, and tools. I'd say don't pick a job just for the title. I'd show them what I do with the tools, because kids pick things up from watching.

say: We have time, so let's **build properly** and plan which roles will still need people.
I'd talk about the **opportunity** as well as the risk.
think: With ten years I can **pivot** into something I choose.
The thinking part of my job goes, but I'd have time to see where the **dust lands**.
do: Start a small **consulting practice** around 2030 and invest in index funds.
Keep my skills **fresh**, which is my insurance.
feel: **Calm**, since a far-off date makes it a long project.
S4.quote: Moving early means I'm choosing, not being chosen. It's a bit like selling a house before the market turns, you get the better price.
fieldNote: Iris is only **uneasy** here: ten years gives her time to pivot, and she wants to be choosing, not chosen.
She wants to **model tools** for her kids rather than lecture.

steps.text: Start a small consulting practice around 2030
Put a monthly amount into index funds
Keep up with new AI tools every quarter

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build anything new. What would help is a transition payment, a retraining scheme with real jobs at the end, and a tax setup that doesn't punish people for starting small businesses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that being good with the tools doesn't make you safe. People assume if you use it daily you're protected. I think I'm actually more aware of the risk, because I see how good it is.

headlineQuote: People assume if you use it daily you're protected. I think I'm actually more aware of the risk, because I see how good it is.
portrait: Iris is a **43-year-old** buyer at an electronics components distributor, with a nurse partner, two kids and a mortgage.
She uses AI **every day**, builds automations and thinks in business plans, cash buffers and early moves.
She knows the tools' speed from demos, so her **worry is informed** and rises sharply in the 2028 world.
She wants to be **choosing, not chosen**, and uses extra time to build consulting and a cash buffer.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most, because there's no time to build anything new.
whatWouldHelp: A **transition payment**, retraining that leads to real jobs and fair rules for small start-ups.
